extracted.intended_audience: Harvard Kennedy School faculty, researchers, students, staff, and external contributors seeking to write publishable op-eds
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting a publishable newspaper/magazine op-ed: how to choose a topic, structure argument, marshal evidence, and match voice and timeliness for the news cycle in 500–1,000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly defined point (single thesis)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Op-eds should have one central, clearly articulated thesis that the piece advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong, unique voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong, unique voice — author's authentic perspective
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's distinct voice and authentic perspective should come through to engage readers and differentiate the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of thinking
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing must be logically organized and readable so the argument is easy to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelling subject — topic readers care about
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a subject with clear reader interest or public relevance; the topic should matter to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow focus / appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a focused scope that can be effectively treated in the typical op-ed length (roughly 500–1,000 words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to current events
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect to current events — peg to recent news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie the piece to recent news or developments so it has immediacy and relevance to the news cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely angle on enduring topic
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when addressing long-standing issues, provide a timely hook or angle that makes the piece newsworthy now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: make a call to action
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Op-eds can be structured to urge readers or policymakers toward a specific action; clearly state what should be done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: offer concrete recommendations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, lay out specific, actionable recommendations as part of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument: illustrate a point of view
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece can aim to persuade by vividly illustrating a perspective or interpretation of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-subject focus
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick to one clear subject or thrust rather than trying to cover multiple, unrelated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and rebut opposing views
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly mention opposing views with rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention counterarguments briefly and rebut them to strengthen credibility and preempt objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts, statistics, historical context, quotations and citations, personal observation, source data
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with appropriate evidence—data, facts, history, quotes, or first-hand observation—and cite sources when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritativeness / credentials
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should have relevant expertise or credibility on the topic to persuade editors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of thesis
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a fresh, original argument or framing rather than restating well-worn positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical relevance — peg to current news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the piece is clearly relevant to current conversations or events; editors look for topicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument should have implications for the broader public or public debate, not just a personal anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear conclusion / takeaway
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear conclusion — what should reader think/do?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End with a clear statement of the intended takeaway or the action/reasoning you want the reader to adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterargument acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing opposing views briefly enhances credibility and persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make every sentence count; be economical with words to cover substance within the short word limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and personality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let personality and distinct phrasing come through so the piece feels human and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific examples — anchored in concrete cases
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor arguments in concrete, specific examples rather than abstraction to improve persuasiveness and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic value — contributes to public debate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pieces that advance civic discussion or inform public decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form distinctions and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of opinion have different newsworthiness expectations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the differences among editorial, op-ed, column, and letter-to-the-editor formats, and tailor content and tone accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial (form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials express the publication's institutional stance and are typically written by the editorial board; expectations differ from op-eds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Op-ed (form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Op-eds are by outside contributors and are attributed; the piece should reflect the author's unique perspective and credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column (form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columns are recurring pieces by a named writer and may build a distinct persona or ongoing argument over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter to the editor (form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letter to editor — Brief reader response
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters are short reader responses and are expected to be concise and reactive to published content.
